title: Uniform density of open-normal quotient functions
statement:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff topological group with a basis of open normal subgroups at the identity: for every open neighbourhood $W$ of $1$ there is an open normal subgroup $U\subseteq W$. Let $B$ be a normed field, with norm topology, and let $C(K,B)$ carry the supremum norm. Define $D\subseteq C(K,B)$ to be the set of functions factoring through $\pi_U:K\to K/U$ for some open normal subgroup $U$. Then $K$ is totally disconnected, meaning that every connected subset has at most one point. For every finite discrete set $F$ and every continuous $g:K\to F$, there is an open normal subgroup $U$ and a function $\bar g:K/U\to F$ with $g=\bar g\circ\pi_U$. For every $f\in C(K,B)$ and every real $\epsilon>0$, there are an open normal subgroup $U$ and a function $b:K/U\to B$ such that the continuous function $d=b\circ\pi_U$ satisfies
$$\|f-d\|_\infty<\epsilon.$$
Equivalently, $D$ is dense in $C(K,B)$ for the supremum norm. No completeness or nonarchimedean hypothesis on $B$, and no countability or metrizability hypothesis on $K$, is required. All spaces use [def-weil-size-convention].

proof.text: Every left coset $xU$ of an open subgroup is open, since left translation is a homeomorphism; its complement is the union of the other open cosets, so it is also closed. Given $x\ne y$, Hausdorffness makes $K\setminus\{x^{-1}y\}$ an open neighbourhood of $1$. Choose an open normal $U$ inside it. Then $xU$ contains $x$ and excludes $y$. A connected subset containing both points would be separated by its intersections with $xU$ and its complement. Thus every connected subset has at most one point, as required.

proof.text: For any open normal $U$, the cosets cover compact $K$ by disjoint nonempty open sets. A finite subcover therefore includes every coset, so $K/U$ is finite. Give it the discrete topology. The inverse image under $\pi_U$ of any subset is a union of open cosets, so $\pi_U$ is continuous. Every map from $K/U$ to any topological space is continuous, and hence so is its composite with $\pi_U$.

proof.text: By step 1, $K$ is a profinite group in the compact Hausdorff totally disconnected sense. Apply [lem-exc-coinduced-functions-open-stabilizer] to the given continuous $g:K\to F$, with $F$ discrete. It gives an open normal $U$ with $g(xu)=g(x)$ for all $x\in K$ and $u\in U$. Define $\bar g(xU)=g(x)$. If $xU=yU$ then $y=xu$ for some $u\in U$, so the displayed invariance proves that this value is well defined. Consequently $g=\bar g\circ\pi_U$.

proof.text: Fix $f\in C(K,B)$ and $\epsilon>0$. The set $S=\{(v,w)\in B\times B:\|v-w\|<\epsilon/2\}$ is open and contains the diagonal, by continuity of the norm and $\epsilon/2>0$. Apply [lem-sfb-profinite-finite-map-approximation], using compactness, Hausdorffness and step 1, with $X=K$ and $V=B$. Obtain a finite discrete set $F$, continuous $g:K\to F$ and $h:F\to B$ such that $\|f(x)-h(g(x))\|<\epsilon/2$ for every $x$. Step 3 supplies $U$ and $\bar g:K/U\to F$. Set $b=h\circ\bar g$ and $d=b\circ\pi_U=h\circ g$. Step 2 makes $d$ continuous. Taking the supremum of the pointwise bounds gives $\|f-d\|_\infty\leq\epsilon/2<\epsilon$. Thus each open norm ball about each $f$ meets $D$, which is precisely density. This argument uses neither completeness of $B$ nor countability of $K$.
